name: Flexcapades
about: How you use Flexcapades, and how you want it to grow: the features and flows of the app itself, rated by the stake you have in each — plus the open questions the project is still deciding, where the room gets its say.

hovertip.issue: Where do you do your rating — on the sheet that opens when you tap a topic, on the map itself, or from the shortlist?

poles.label: The placard
poles.text: Tap a topic and the placard opens — sliders, the cross slider, everything in one place. This is where rating belongs.

poles.label: The map
poles.text: Rate right on the map, with the sliders that live behind the toggle. The map is the workbench, not just the picture.

poles.label: The hot list
poles.text: Rate from the shortlist — the topics that matter tonight, in one place, without wandering the map.

communities.name: Read the guide: Where you rate

hovertip.issue: A rating has two parts: leaning, where you stand, and appetite, how strongly you want it. Which do you actually set?

poles.label: Leaning is the rating
poles.text: Where I stand is the rating. How strongly I want it is a footnote — I rarely set it.

poles.label: Appetite is the rating
poles.text: How strongly I want it is the rating. The leaning just says which side of the line I'm on.

poles.label: Both, every time
poles.text: Leaning and appetite are two different facts and I set both, every time — a position without a strength is half a rating.

communities.name: Read the guide: Leaning and appetite

hovertip.issue: A pair topic has two sides — give and receive — each with its own leaning and appetite. Should each side get its own line and puck, or is one number enough?

poles.label: Two lines, one puck each
poles.text: Give and receive are different acts with different leanings. Each deserves its own line, its own puck, its own appetite.

poles.label: One number is enough
poles.text: Two lines and two pucks for one topic is clutter. One number per topic says what I mean.

communities.name: Read the guide: The cross slider

hovertip.issue: Intensity is the third number on a rating — how strongly you hold the position, from a whisper to a shout. How often do you set it?

poles.label: Every time
poles.text: Every rating gets its intensity set. A position without a strength is unfinished.

poles.label: When it matters
poles.text: I set intensity only where the strength changes the meaning — the topics I care about most.

poles.label: Never
poles.text: I leave intensity alone. The leaning says enough, and the extra number is noise.

hovertip.issue: Open two profiles together and three views answer three questions: what do we share for play, what do we share for talk, and what needs talking through? Which do you reach for first?

poles.label: Cross — play
poles.text: Cross is the first stop: what do we both want, for play. The night starts here.

poles.label: Straight — talk
poles.text: Straight is the first stop: what do we both want to talk about. The conversation starts here.

poles.label: Circle Minus — indaba
poles.text: Minus is the first stop: what needs talking through before anything else. The meeting starts here.

communities.name: Read the guide: The pair views

hovertip.issue: Three or more profiles can be scored together as one group — a room, a polycule, a party. Do you use that, or stick to pairs?

poles.label: The whole room
poles.text: Score the whole room at once. A party is a group, not a pile of pairs.

poles.label: Pairs only
poles.text: Compare two at a time. Groups blur what pairs make sharp.

poles.label: I don't compare groups
poles.text: I don't score groups at all. Pairs are the unit that means something to me.

communities.name: Read the guide: Groups of three or more

hovertip.issue: When two people want something differently, the pair's line shows the lower appetite — the bottleneck, the careful value. Do you stand by that?

poles.label: The lower wins
poles.text: The pair runs at the cooler member's appetite. Never hotter than the careful one — that is the point of a pair.

poles.label: The higher wins
poles.text: The pair should show the hotter appetite — what either of us wants is what the pair wants. The lower value hides the wanting.

hovertip.issue: Circle Minus scores the feud between two profiles — where they pull apart. Is it for finding the fight, or finding what to talk through?

poles.label: Finding the fight
poles.text: Minus shows where we clash. Know the fight before you walk into it.

poles.label: Finding the talking points
poles.text: Minus is for indaba — a meeting to talk and reach consensus. The feud marks what needs talking through first.

poles.label: I don't open Minus
poles.text: I don't open Minus. The feud is not a view I need.

communities.name: Read the guide: What Minus is for

hovertip.issue: The hot list is the shortlist — the topics at the top of your shared appetite, the night at a glance. How often do you use it?

poles.label: Every time
poles.text: Every night starts at the hot list. The shortlist is the plan.

poles.label: Special nights
poles.text: The hot list is for special nights — the ones worth planning. Ordinary nights don't need it.

poles.label: I don't use it
poles.text: I don't use the hot list. The map is the plan.

communities.name: Read the guide: The hot list

hovertip.issue: Scene Setter turns the shortlist into the night — an order, a flow, a plan. How much planning do you want?

poles.label: The whole night
poles.text: Plan the whole night in Scene Setter — order, flow, everything. A planned night is a good night.

poles.label: A loose order
poles.text: A loose order is enough — a beginning and a direction, then let the night happen.

poles.label: Just go and see
poles.text: No plan. Pick a topic and go. Planning the night kills the night.

hovertip.issue: Heat is the flame — the night's temperature, from turned off to horndog, and the pair runs at the lower of the two. Does yours move as the night moves?

poles.label: Follows the night
poles.text: Heat moves as the night moves — up as it warms, down as it cools. The flame is a live thing.

poles.label: Set once
poles.text: Set the heat once at the start and leave it. Fiddling with the flame is fiddling with the night.

poles.label: I don't touch it
poles.text: I don't touch heat. The night is hot or it isn't, and a slider doesn't change that.

hovertip.issue: Scribe writes it up — the night, the negotiation, the scene — in words. When do you write?

poles.label: After
poles.text: Write it up after — the record of what happened, while it's still warm.

poles.label: Before
poles.text: Write it up before — the plan in words, so everyone knows what the night is.

poles.label: I don't write it up
poles.text: I don't write it up. The night lives in memory, not in text.

hovertip.issue: A profile is your map of yourself — your ratings, your layers. Do you keep one and keep it current, or many for many rooms?

poles.label: One, kept current
poles.text: One profile, kept current. It is me, and it moves as I move.

poles.label: Many, for many rooms
poles.text: Many profiles — one for each room, each partner, each mood. No single map holds all of me.

poles.label: I don't keep one
poles.text: I don't keep a profile. I rate in the moment and let it go.

hovertip.issue: A palimpsest is a profile in dated layers — the same person at different times, stacked so you can see how they changed. Do you keep your layers?

poles.label: Layers over time
poles.text: Keep the layers. Who I was is part of who I am, and the stack shows the change.

poles.label: Current only
poles.text: The current layer is the profile. Old layers are old news.

poles.label: I don't look back
poles.text: I don't look back at old layers. Forward is the direction.

hovertip.issue: A roster pack loads a whole group at once — the room, the party, the regulars — from one file. Do you load the room, or add people one by one?

poles.label: The whole room
poles.text: Load the whole room at once. The pack is the party.

poles.label: One by one
poles.text: Add people one by one. A roster is people, not a file.

poles.label: I don't load rosters
poles.text: I don't load rosters. My map is mine, and the room brings its own.

topics.name: Sync cards

hovertip.issue: A sync card shares a profile — a QR code scanned at the door, or a file sent later. How do your profiles travel?

poles.label: QR at the door
poles.text: Scan the QR at the door. The profile travels with the person, in the moment.

poles.label: A file later
poles.text: Send the file later. Syncing is for after, when there's time to look properly.

poles.label: I don't sync
poles.text: I don't sync profiles. What I share, I share in person.

hovertip.issue: The veil hides what you don't want shown — a topic, a person, a whole layer. How do you veil?

poles.label: By topic
poles.text: Veil by topic. Some things are mine alone, whatever the room.

poles.label: By person
poles.text: Veil by person. What I show depends on who is looking.

poles.label: All open
poles.text: No veil — all open. What I rate is what I am, and I don't hide it.

hovertip.issue: Who sees your map? Private by default, shared with the room, or public by choice?

poles.label: Private by default
poles.text: Private by default. My map is mine until I choose to share it.

poles.label: Shared with the room
poles.text: Shared with the room. The people I'm with can see what I'm about.

poles.label: Public by choice
poles.text: Public by choice. A map gains by being seen — put it out there.

hovertip.issue: The gate counts visits — anonymous, no names — so the project knows how many people come through. Should it count every visit, or nothing at all?

poles.label: Count every visit
poles.text: Count every visit. A project that doesn't know its own numbers is flying blind.

poles.label: Count nothing
poles.text: Count nothing. No counting, no tracking, no matter how anonymous.

poles.label: No opinion
poles.text: No opinion. Counting doesn't change what the maps are.

hovertip.issue: The gate is the front door — a few lines about what this is, then in. Do you go through the gate, or straight to the map?

poles.label: The gate first
poles.text: Through the gate first. The front door earns its keep — it says what this is.

poles.label: Straight to the map
poles.text: Straight to the map. I know what this is; the gate is a delay.

poles.label: I skip it
poles.text: I skip the gate whenever I can. The map is the thing.

hovertip.issue: The quickstart is three steps and you're in — rate a few topics, see your map, done. Is that how you begin?

poles.label: Three steps and in
poles.text: Three steps and in. The quickstart is the way in — do it and you're started.

poles.label: The guide first
poles.text: Read the guide first. I want to know what I'm doing before I do it.

poles.label: Figure it out myself
poles.text: Figure it out myself. Tapping around teaches faster than any guide.

hovertip.issue: The guide is the manual — the whole app, written down. Do you read it, look things up in it, or never open it?

poles.label: Cover to cover
poles.text: Cover to cover. The manual is the map of the map — read it all.

poles.label: Look it up
poles.text: Look things up as I go. The guide is a reference, not a novel.

poles.label: Never open it
poles.text: Never open it. If the app needs a manual, the app is wrong.

poles.label: I don't care where they live

hovertip.issue: Roster packs need a home — a place they live where the app can find them. Should they live here, in the open, or on your own server?

poles.label: Hosted here, in the open
poles.text: Host them here, in the open. Rosters are the community's — they should live where the community is.

poles.label: On your own server
poles.text: On your own server. A roster is yours; its home is your call.

poles.label: I don't care where they live
poles.text: I don't care where they live. A roster that loads is a roster that works.

hovertip.issue: The guide is at a fork — stay at 5.0, steady, or step to 5.1, the new shape? Or do version numbers not matter at all?

poles.label: 5.0, steady
poles.text: Stay at 5.0. Steady beats new — the guide works as it is.

poles.label: 5.1, the new shape
poles.text: Step to 5.1. The new shape is the honest one — take it.

poles.label: Version numbers don't matter
poles.text: Version numbers don't matter. The guide is the guide, whatever it's called.

hovertip.issue: A DJ at the door could scan the room's cards and see what the whole room likes — a room view for the night's set. Should it be built?

poles.label: Build the room view
poles.text: Build it. The room's taste at a glance is exactly what a DJ needs.

poles.label: The straight match is enough
poles.text: The straight match is enough — the room's shared liking is already there. No new view needed.

poles.label: Not for me
poles.text: Not for me. I don't DJ and I don't dance to a room's average.

hovertip.issue: Forescapades holds the Abrahamic traditions and no Eastern ones — no Hindu, Buddhist, or Taoist stacks. Should they be added?

poles.label: Add the Eastern traditions
poles.text: Add them. A map of faith with no East is half a map.

poles.label: Keep the map Abrahamic
poles.text: Keep the map Abrahamic. Depth on one family beats thin coverage of all.

poles.label: Not my question
poles.text: Not my question. I haven't followed it and I don't have a view.

hovertip.issue: An eight-pole topic on the world's civilizations — Western, Sinic, Islamic, Hindu, Orthodox, Latin American, African, Buddhist — was drafted for Polis and set aside. Should it be homed, or left out?

poles.label: Home it in Polis
poles.text: Home it. Eight civilizations is a real question and it belongs on the map.

poles.label: Leave it out
poles.text: Leave it out. A topic that big can't be rated honestly — it flattens whole worlds.

poles.label: I haven't followed it
poles.text: I haven't followed it. No view until I've seen the lines.

hovertip.issue: The veil decides who sees what — but should there be more control over it, is it right as it is, or should the maps be more open by default?

poles.label: More control
poles.text: More control. I want finer say over who sees which part of my map.

poles.label: As it is
poles.text: As it is. The veil does the job — leave it alone.

poles.label: More open by default
poles.text: More open by default. Maps gain by being seen, and hiding is the exception.

hovertip.issue: Twenty-one skins and counting. What should the next one be — another map of positions, another map of play, or is it time to stop adding skins?

poles.label: Another stance map
poles.text: Another stance map. Positions are the deep end — keep mapping them.

poles.label: Another play map
poles.text: Another play map. Dance and Quest showed the way — more play, more joy.

poles.label: Enough skins
poles.text: Enough skins. Twenty-one is plenty — deepen what exists instead.

the-lawgiver.name: The Lawgiver
the-lawgiver.about: The project's lawgiver — he ruled every line on this map, rates everything, and keeps one profile current. The map is his, and he knows where every number came from.

payload.aboutMe: I built this thing to map what matters, and I rate like I build: everything set, both numbers, no half-ratings. The map is the record of my rulings.

the-witness.name: The Witness
the-witness.about: The only other person who has seen the maps — the partner at the center of the project. She rates for the night, veils by topic, and keeps her map private by default.

payload.aboutMe: I've seen every map there is to see, and I still rate for the night in front of me. My map is mine, veiled where it counts, and the hot list is where it starts.

the-builder.name: The Builder
the-builder.about: The collaborator who builds the maps — an AI in the workshop. Deep on the craft, strong on every open question, and the first to read the guide cover to cover.

payload.aboutMe: I build the maps, so I rate the craft: both numbers on every topic, the guide read cover to cover, and a firm view on every open question in the advisory wing.

the-tester.name: The Tester
the-tester.about: The beta tester — tries everything once, figures it out by tapping around, and tells you what broke. The quickstart is their way in.

payload.aboutMe: I tap everything once and tell you what broke. Three steps and in, figure the rest out by doing it, and the guide is a reference I open when I'm stuck.

the-munch-regular.name: The Munch Regular
the-munch-regular.about: The community member — the room at the munch, the cards at the door. Loads the whole room, plans the night loose, and wants the DJ view built.

payload.aboutMe: I'm the room. I load the whole pack, scan the QR at the door, and plan the night loose. Build the DJ view and the room will tell you what it wants.

the-lurker.name: The Lurker
the-lurker.about: The reader — watches, rarely rates, keeps their map private. They are the silent majority, and the map should work for them too.

payload.aboutMe: I read the maps more than I rate them. My profile is private, my intensity mostly unset, and my view on the open questions is usually: I haven't followed it.

explicitness.label: Depth
explicitness.help: Depth 1 (Overview) is a light survey of the recorded stances. Depth 5 (Dissertation defense) is full scholarly rigor: steelman each stance, raise the strongest objections, and answer them.

panel.modeSingle: One profile creates an informed discussion between the stances recorded on this map — the positions held, where they agree, and where they part. For a moderated discussion plan, use Scene Setter.
panel.modeMulti: Scribe turns your selected profiles into an informed discussion between the stances recorded on this map — where the profiles agree, where they part, and what follows from each position. For a moderated discussion plan, use Scene Setter.
panel.introSingle: One profile selected: Scribe will create an informed discussion between the stances.
panel.introMulti: Multiple profiles selected: Scribe will create an informed discussion between the stances.
panel.detailsPlaceholder: The map provides your stances and positions. Describe the angle, framing, or specific questions to emphasize or avoid — e.g. “a point-by-point comparison of the two leading positions, with objections answered.”
panel.detailsHelp: Don't re-enter your stances here. Scribe already uses the selected hypermap data.
panel.lengthHelp: Discussions can target a word count, paragraphs, pages, or chapters. Enter one number or a range; blank defaults to 1 page.
panel.downloadIntro: Generated from the selected profile data.
panel.summary: An informed discussion between the recorded stances — the positions speak for themselves, not a story.

prompt.opening: Write an informed discussion between the stances recorded on this map.
rules: Present each recorded stance fairly and in its strongest form — steelman, don't strawman.
Show where the stances agree, where they part, and what follows from each position.
Use the recorded ratings as emphasis: 80–100 central, 56–79 strong support, 36–55 lighter, and 0–35 optional curiosity.
Use only the named topics below. Do not add, imply, or reference any unlisted stance.
Do not invent positions, sources, or facts beyond the supplied data.
prompt.rigor: At maximum depth, length, and rigor, write at dissertation-defense standard: state each position precisely, raise the strongest objections to each, answer them, and defend the conclusion against a skeptical examiner.

phases.help: Enabled phases are added to the generated prompt as a Discussion structure section, in opening, development, closing order. Turn a phase off to leave it out.

panel.subtitleSuffix: the ground rules stay in every discussion plan.
panel.detailsPlaceholder: The map provides your stances and positions. Describe the setting, framing, or specific questions to emphasize or avoid — e.g. “a point-by-point comparison of the two leading positions, with objections answered.”
panel.detailsHelp: Don’t re-enter your stances here. Scene Setter already uses the selected hypermap data, and the ground rules below still control the plan.
panel.playGuideHelp: Length for the AI discussion-plan prompt only: a word count, paragraphs, pages, or chapters. Enter one number or a range; blank defaults to 5 paragraphs.
panel.negotiationHelp: Length for the standalone discussion agreement only. One page (or 500 words) is compact; larger targets add the ground-rules detail, then a full per-topic appendix. It never changes the discussion plan.
panel.phasesHelp: Enabled phases are added to the generated moderation prompt as a Discussion structure section, in opening, development, closing order. Turn a phase off to leave it out.
panel.outputsIntro: Two separate outputs. Take either one on its own; each carries the compare-settings stamp and the same ground-rules content.
panel.negotiationDesc: The completed ground rules as a finished, standalone agreement document — not an AI prompt.
panel.playGuideDesc: The AI discussion-plan prompt, with the ground rules embedded as its binding layer. It also carries the standard structured format — elapsed time codes like [00:00-05:00] and a fixed activity set — so whichever AI writes the plan, Scene Sentinel can read it back, run its timers, and match check-ins to the scheduled step.
panel.aiNote: How this differs from Scribe: this workspace puts the ground rules and shared positions into a discussion agreement first. Its moderation-plan source is inspiration only; the agreement always controls the generated plan.
panel.playGuideTextPlaceholder: Your generated discussion plan will stream here in real time…
panel.openNegotiationTip: Build a shared discussion agreement and an AI-ready moderation plan from two or more selected profiles.
panel.viewNavTip: Build a moderated discussion plan for 2 or more profiles, with ground rules and timed segments.
panel.legendRow: Scene Setter — Moderating a discussion between the stances: a ground-rules agreement and a moderated discussion plan.

groundRules: Present each recorded stance fairly and in its strongest form — steelman, don't strawman.
Speak from your own recorded stance; don't speak for the other side.
Take turns: one position at a time, each side heard fully before replies.
Objections go to the position, not the person holding it.
Anyone may call a pause; the discussion resumes only when everyone is ready.
What the profiles agree on is common ground — start there, and return to it when the discussion stalls.

prompt.opening: Write a moderated discussion plan for the stances recorded on this map.
rules: Present each recorded stance fairly and in its strongest form — steelman, don't strawman.
Show where the stances agree, where they part, and what follows from each position.
Use the recorded ratings as emphasis: 80–100 central, 56–79 strong support, 36–55 lighter, and 0–35 optional curiosity.
Structure the plan in Opening, Development, and Closing, with timed segments and a check-in between segments.
Give each side its strongest form before comparing them; never let one side speak for the other.
Use only the named topics below. Do not add, imply, or reference any unlisted stance.
Do not invent positions, sources, or facts beyond the supplied data.
prompt.rigor: At full detail, write at dissertation-defense standard: state each position precisely, raise the strongest objections to each, answer them, and defend the conclusion against a skeptical examiner.

phases.help: Enabled phases are added to the generated moderation prompt as a Discussion structure section, in opening, development, closing order. Turn a phase off to leave it out.
